title: Targeted Operations and Forced Replacement
intro: Sometimes you need to act on exactly one resource — recreate a broken server, or preview changes to one component. These are sharp tools: useful in emergencies, dangerous as a habit.

steps.prompt: A worker instance is in a bad state and needs to be rebuilt from scratch. Preview replacing only aws_instance.worker[1].
steps.explanation: -/+ means destroy then create. Only this one instance is affected.
steps.why: This replaces the old 'terraform taint' command, which was deprecated because it modified state immediately — before anyone reviewed a plan. -replace only takes effect as part of a normal, reviewable plan/apply.

steps.fake_output:
aws_instance.worker[1]: Destroying...
aws_instance.worker[1]: Creating...
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 1 destroyed.
steps.explanation: A fresh instance replaces the broken one.
steps.why: If the resource has create_before_destroy in its lifecycle block, the new one is built before the old one is removed — worth setting on anything that serves traffic.

steps.prompt: Preview changes to ONLY the security group, ignoring everything else in the configuration.
steps.explanation: Terraform warns you: this is a partial view.
steps.why: -target is for emergencies and debugging, not routine use. It deliberately ignores other pending changes, so your real infrastructure and code can quietly drift apart. Always follow up with a full, untargeted plan.

steps.prompt: Check for pending changes in a way a CI job can act on automatically: exit code 0 = no changes, 2 = changes present, 1 = error.
steps.fake_output:
Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.
(exit code: 2)
steps.explanation: Exit code 2 signals that changes exist.
steps.why: This is the foundation of scheduled drift detection: run it nightly against production, and alert on exit code 2. That catches manual console changes (terraform-incident-001) within a day instead of at the next deploy.
